title: Resistivity of wires from a V-I graph
objective: To plot a graph of potential difference versus current for a given wire.
To determine its resistance from the slope of the graph.
To calculate the resistivity of the material of the wire.

theory.statement: Ohm's law states that the current flowing through a conductor is directly proportional to the potential difference across its ends, provided its physical conditions such as temperature remain unchanged. Hence V = IR, where the constant R is the resistance.
theory.derivationNote: A graph of V against I is therefore a straight line through the origin whose slope equals R. The resistance of a uniform wire is R = ρL/A, where L is its length and A = πD²/4 its area of cross-section. Hence ρ = RA/L = RπD²/(4L). Resistivity depends only on the material, not on the length or thickness.
keyEquations: R = slope of the V-I graph

apparatus.name: Specimen wire
apparatus.why: The conductor whose resistivity is measured

apparatus.name: Battery / battery eliminator
apparatus.why: Drives a steady current through the circuit

apparatus.name: Ammeter
apparatus.why: Measures the current; connected IN SERIES

apparatus.name: Voltmeter
apparatus.why: Measures the p.d. across the wire; connected IN PARALLEL

apparatus.name: Rheostat
apparatus.why: Varies the current so several readings can be taken

apparatus.name: One-way key
apparatus.why: Breaks the circuit between readings so the wire does not heat

apparatus.name: Screw gauge
apparatus.why: Measures the diameter of the wire

apparatus.name: Metre scale
apparatus.why: Measures the length of the wire between the terminals

apparatus.name: Sand paper
apparatus.why: Cleans the insulating oxide layer from the wire ends

procedure.text: Clean the ends of the specimen wire with sand paper and measure its length L and diameter D.
Connect the ammeter IN SERIES with the wire, battery, key and rheostat.
Connect the voltmeter IN PARALLEL across the two ends of the specimen wire.
Insert the key and adjust the rheostat so a small current flows. Note the ammeter and voltmeter readings.
Shift the rheostat and take at least five sets of readings over the working range.
Take the key out between readings so the wire does not become hot.
Plot V on the y-axis against I on the x-axis and draw the best-fit straight line through the origin.
Find the slope; this is the resistance R. Calculate ρ = RπD²/(4L).

steps: Slope of the V-I graph gives R in ohm

expectedResult.quantity: Resistivity of the material of the wire
expectedResult.statement: The V-I graph is a straight line through the origin, verifying Ohm's law. The slope gives the resistance and the resistivity of constantan is found to be about 4.9 × 10⁻⁷ Ω·m.

safety: Take the key out of the circuit between readings — a continuously flowing current heats the wire and changes its resistance.
Never connect the ammeter in parallel with the wire: it will short-circuit the cell and can be damaged.
Do not exceed the range of the ammeter or the voltmeter.
Check that all connections are tight; loose connections cause sparking and unsteady readings.
sourcesOfError: Heating of the wire raises its resistance, so the graph curves upward at large currents.
Zero error in the ammeter or voltmeter not corrected.
Parallax error while reading the pointer of a moving-coil meter.
Resistance of the connecting wires and of loose contacts included in the measurement.
The voltmeter draws a small current, so the ammeter reads slightly more than the current in the wire.

viva.question: State Ohm's law and its condition of validity.
viva.expectedConcept: The current through a conductor is directly proportional to the potential difference across it, provided physical conditions such as temperature remain constant.
viva.answerLogic: V = IR with the constant-temperature condition.
viva.commonMisconception: Stating V = IR without the condition on temperature.

viva.question: Why is the ammeter connected in series and the voltmeter in parallel?
viva.expectedConcept: An ammeter has very low resistance and must carry the whole current, so it goes in series; a voltmeter has very high resistance and must not divert current, so it goes across the component in parallel.
viva.commonMisconception: Reversing the two, which short-circuits the wire or chokes the current.

viva.question: What is resistivity? On what factors does it depend?
viva.expectedConcept: Resistivity is the resistance of a conductor of unit length and unit area of cross-section. It depends on the nature of the material and its temperature, but not on the length or thickness of the specimen.
viva.commonMisconception: Saying resistivity depends on the length or area of the wire.

viva.question: What does the slope of the V-I graph give?
viva.expectedConcept: The slope of the potential difference versus current graph is the resistance of the wire in ohm.
viva.commonMisconception: Taking the slope of the I-V graph as R instead of 1/R.

viva.question: Why is constantan or nichrome used rather than copper for this experiment?
viva.expectedConcept: They have a much higher resistivity and a very low temperature coefficient of resistance, so they give a measurable p.d. and their resistance hardly changes on heating.
viva.commonMisconception: Thinking copper is avoided only because it is expensive.

viva.question: Why should the key be taken out between readings?
viva.expectedConcept: To prevent the wire from heating. A rise in temperature increases the resistance and the V-I graph would no longer be a straight line.
viva.commonMisconception: Saying it is only to save the battery.

viva.question: What is the effect on resistance if the wire is stretched to twice its length?
viva.expectedConcept: The length doubles and the area halves, so the resistance becomes four times the original value; the resistivity is unchanged.

viva.question: Two wires of the same material have different diameters. Do they have the same resistance? The same resistivity?
viva.expectedConcept: Their resistances differ because R depends on the area of cross-section, but their resistivities are equal since it is the same material at the same temperature.
viva.answerLogic: R geometry dependent, ρ material property.
viva.commonMisconception: Assuming a thicker wire has a smaller resistivity.

viva.question: Why must the V-I graph pass through the origin?
viva.expectedConcept: When no current flows there can be no potential difference across a pure resistance, so the line must start at the origin. An intercept indicates a zero error or a thermo-emf.
viva.commonMisconception: Accepting a visible intercept as normal.

preLab.question: An ammeter must be connected:
preLab.feedback: An ammeter has almost no resistance and must carry the full current, so it goes in series.

preLab.question: The resistivity of a wire depends on:
preLab.feedback: Resistivity is a property of the material at a given temperature, independent of the dimensions of the specimen.

preLab.question: The instrument used to measure the diameter of the wire is:
preLab.feedback: A screw gauge with least count 0.001 cm is needed for a wire less than a millimetre thick.

duringLab.question: Connect the ammeter in series and the voltmeter in parallel.
Record at least five sets of readings at different rheostat settings.
Check that your V/I ratio stays nearly constant.

postLab.question: State the resistance of the wire obtained from your graph (Ω).
postLab.feedback: For a 100 cm constantan wire of diameter 0.4 mm, R is about 3.9 Ω.

postLab.question: Your V-I graph is a straight line through the origin. This verifies:
postLab.feedback: Direct proportionality between V and I is exactly Ohm's law.

postLab.question: If you halve the length of the wire, the resistivity you calculate should:
postLab.feedback: Resistance halves, but ρ = RA/L is unchanged because it is a property of the material.

scientificValidation.formula: V = IR; R = slope of V-I; ρ = RπD²/(4L)
assumptions: Wire is ohmic over the range used
Temperature constant unless heating is enabled
Ammeter resistance negligible, voltmeter resistance very large
scientificValidation.unitSystem: SI; L in cm and D in mm on the bench, converted to m for ρ
edgeCases: Ammeter in parallel short-circuits the wire — blocked with explanation
Voltmeter in series chokes the current to nearly zero — blocked with explanation
High current heats the wire and curves the graph
expectedBehaviour: V directly proportional to I at constant temperature
R doubles when the length doubles; R quarters when the diameter doubles
ρ unchanged by geometry, recovered within 5%
